parts.text: Its success belonged to a burgeoning taste for “books of secrets”, recipe-like instructional texts that taught everything from

and alchemy to brewing and beekeeping.

Originating in Italy, and published throughout the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, the most popular of these works were continually translated and reprinted throughout Europe. They are now recognised as exerting

influence on contemporary scientific culture.

Whether providing alchemical routes to the philosopher’s stone or the recipe for a nutritious stew, books like A Thousand Notable Things thrived on the promise of revealing hidden “secrets” about nature’s

workings.

Of course, there was no guarantee that everything Lupton suggested would work: whether sleeping on your right side during pregnancy really meant the baby would be female, or that dreaming of eagles flying overhead was necessarily a sign of

good fortune. Sheer efficacy alone wasn’t the point. The appeal lay in the wonder, curiosity and amusement that accompanied practical instruction.

If some passages sound absurd or downright dangerous to modern ears (henbane and mercury are highly

), consider that much of Lupton’s material was cutting-edge in its day. His most cited source was Antoine Mizauld, a Parisian medical professor and advisor to French queen Marguerite de Valois.

Even though the vitality of astrology, occult science and

medicine waned over the book’s 250-year lifespan, the deeply human concerns it addressed proved enduringly popular.

Personal copies

We know that contemporary readers found Lupton’s eclectic material engaging thanks to their annotations in personal copies,

few of which remain today.

One survivor from 1612, now in the Glasgow University Library, is marked with small crosses at passages on lameness, heart trouble, ulcers, meat eating and stomach problems. We might speculate that its owner was managing

of dietary issues or gout. So too are gout cures underlined in a copy owned by the 17th-century book collector Frances Wolfreston.

Another reader pencilled crosses next to 38 predominantly medical passages in their 1706 copy, including

for head and toothaches, burning eyes, shortness of breath, sore throat and insomnia.

Others were more selective. One copy in the Wellcome Collection is marked only occasionally, including at an anecdote about a German farmer who died with terrible pain in his side. A
cut him open to find large pieces of wood and four steel knives, afflictions that were blamed on the Devil.
